name: Cold exposure for mood

lead: Cold exposure means deliberately taking cold showers or plunging into cold water to feel more alert, resilient and disciplined. In looksmaxxing circles it is grouped with habits that build willpower and energy, so routines like training and grooming stay consistent.

Proponents attribute the effects to the body's stress response to cold and to the act of voluntarily doing something uncomfortable. Cold-water immersion is best studied for athletic recovery: a Cochrane review found some evidence it reduces delayed-onset muscle soreness and perceived fatigue. A 2024 meta-analysis reported an apparent decline in perceived stress within 12 hours, along with improved sleep and quality-of-life scores, in studies of fair to poor quality. None address appearance.

paras: People end a normal shower with cold water or use a cold plunge or ice bath for a short time, often in the morning or after training. Some pair it with breathing routines such as the Wim Hof Method. It is used daily or several times a week as a habit.

Medical bodies note risks of hypothermia, circulatory shock and sudden cardiac events from cold-water immersion, and the American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician first. Breathing exercises combined with water immersion have been linked in reports to blackout and drowning deaths.

angle.text: Cold showers and plunges are used in looksmaxxing circles as a mood booster and discipline habit that keeps routines like training consistent. Small studies report lower perceived stress and better sleep; none address appearance.

lead: Cold exposure for mood is the practice of using cold showers, ice baths or cold plunges to feel more alert, less stressed and more disciplined. In looksmaxxing and wider self-improvement communities it is treated as a mood and consistency habit: people who feel sharper and more driven tend to keep up the training, sleep, skincare and grooming routines that improve appearance.[1][2] Some also use immersion after workouts to feel fresher for the next session.[1]

Cold-water immersion is best studied as a sports recovery method. A 2012 Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found some evidence that it reduces delayed-onset muscle soreness and perceived fatigue after exercise, and a 2025 meta-analysis reported an apparent decline in perceived stress within 12 hours, along with better sleep and quality-of-life scores, with the underlying studies rated fair to poor quality.[1]

The practice's best-known modern figure is the Dutch athlete Wim Hof, whose method pairs cold exposure with breathing exercises.[3] Health bodies warn about hypothermia, circulatory shock and sudden cardiac events, and the Wim Hof Method has been linked in media and legal reports to drownings.[1][3]

paras: Ice baths, also called cold plunges or cold-water immersion, involve immersing much of the body in cold water for a short time. Athletes use them mainly after training, typically at 10 to 15 degrees C for 10 to 15 minutes; other sources suggest different durations.[1] Physiotherapist Tony Wilson of the University of Southampton has argued that a cold bath at 16 to 24 degrees C works as well as an ice bath, according to Wikipedia.[1]

In mood-focused versions, people use cold showers or plunges as a daily habit. Wikipedia notes that ice baths are increasingly promoted for perceived mental health benefits, including relief of depression symptoms.[1] A T Nation poster in a training log described strategies for keeping up daily cold showers as mornings cooled, framing it as a habit worth sustaining.[2]

Cold-water use is ancient: Wikipedia cites the Edwin Smith Papyrus, believed to date to about 3500 BCE, and says the ancient Greeks used cold immersion for fever and pain. Medical use continued into the late 1950s, and D. H. Clarke applied it to post-exercise recovery in the 1960s.[1] Marathon runner Paula Radcliffe credited ice baths for her 10,000 m win at the 2002 European Championships, which helped popularise them among athletes.[1]

In the 2010s and 2020s the practice moved into mainstream wellness. Wikipedia says ice baths became very popular after discussion by Joe Rogan and guests such as Andrew Huberman, and it notes the 2014 ALS Ice Bucket Challenge, which raised about $16 million in 22 days as a fundraiser rather than a therapy.[1] A 2014 post on cold showers and exercise, framed around the idea that moderate stress drives adaptation, drew a long Hacker News discussion in which some commenters said cold showers wake them up or lift mood and others saw no benefit.[4]

Wim Hof, born 20 April 1959 in Sittard, Netherlands, markets a regimen of willpower, cold exposure and breathing techniques, and holds or has held records for barefoot running on ice and snow, under-ice swimming and prolonged ice contact.[3] He says his first cold experience was jumping into a Beatrixpark canal at 17.[3] Books include Becoming the Iceman (2012) and The Wim Hof Method (2020), and documentaries include Vice's The Super Human World of Wim Hof: The Iceman (2015).[3]

A 2011 study at Radboud University, broadcast on Dutch television on 19 April 2011, examined his abilities, and its researchers Pickkers and Kox are reported to have warned him against overstating health claims.[3] A 2024 meta-analysis of eight studies found possible reduced inflammation via epinephrine, with mixed results for exercise performance and respiratory measures; it rated study quality as very low, citing small samples and 86.4% male participants.[3] Critics have objected to claims that the method helps with rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis and cancer.[3]

No studies found testing cold showers specifically as an appearance intervention. Related research on cold-water immersion is mostly in athletes. A Cochrane review (Bleakley and colleagues, 2012) reported some evidence for reduced soreness and perceived fatigue after exercise, with no good evidence of other benefits.[1] A 2025 meta-analysis of controlled trials, attributed to Cain and colleagues, reported an apparent drop in perceived stress within 12 hours of exposure and improved sleep and quality-of-life scores, but the authors cautioned that the evidence is uncertain.[1]

Studies by Roberts (2015) and Fyfe (2019), and a 2024 meta-analysis by Pinero and colleagues, found that immersion straight after resistance training may blunt anabolic signalling and muscle growth, though the underlying studies were of fair to poor quality.[1]

Wikipedia reports that medical and scientific sources broadly agree ice baths can pose serious risks, including hypothermia, circulatory shock and sudden cardiac death, and cites research on the cold shock response and autonomic conflict.[1] A British woman died in 2022 after cold water therapy in a Derbyshire river.[1] The American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician before cold therapy.[3]

Regarding the Wim Hof Method, reports describe practitioner drownings, including four in 2015 and 2016; relatives and commentators attribute them to breathing exercises that can cause shallow-water blackout.[3] Scott Carney's 2023 documentary linked 13 deaths to the method, and Wikipedia says 32 deaths had been allegedly linked as of March 2024.[3] A December 2022 lawsuit seeking $67 million after a 17-year-old drowned in a California pool was dismissed on 2 July 2024, with the court finding Hof not liable.[3] Scientists criticised the roughly 650 tonnes of ice ordered for the 2024 Paris Olympics, in a British Journal of Sports Medicine editorial reported by The Guardian.[1]

lore.intro: Cold showers and plunges appear in lifting and self-improvement forums as a mood, energy and willpower habit, with the Wim Hof Method as the best-known branded version.[2][4][3]
